find: Shaping processes give a material its form by pouring or injecting it into a mould cavity while it is in a liquid or semi-liquid state — the material fills the cavity and solidifies into the desired shape. The material is not removed; instead, it fills the cavity of the mould and solidifies into the desired shape.
replace: Shaping processes give a material its form using a mould or a pressing tool, without removing material. In casting and injection moulding, molten or softened material fills a mould cavity and solidifies into the desired shape; powder metallurgy compacts and sinters powder.
note: F1: Includes powder metallurgy without misdescribing it as liquid mould filling.

find: Shaping uses a fluid or semi-fluid material that takes the shape of a mould cavity — the material has no fixed form before the process begins.
replace: Shaping uses a mould or a pressing tool to give material its form — casting and injection moulding fill a mould cavity, while powder metallurgy compacts and sinters powder.
note: F1: Preserves the shaping/forming contrast while covering the listed powder process.

find: The material removed becomes waste swarf or offcuts and cannot be recovered, so careful planning minimises excess material loss.
replace: The material removed becomes waste swarf or offcuts. Where possible, these can be collected for recycling, so careful planning minimises material loss.
note: F2: Suitable manufacturing scrap can be recycled.

expect: 1 mark for identifying it as wasting; 1 mark for stating material is removed from the workpiece; 1 mark for a developed point such as the removed material becomes waste swarf that cannot be recovered, or that the starting block must be larger than the finished part. [3 marks]
value: 1 mark for identifying it as wasting; 1 mark for stating material is removed from the workpiece; 1 mark for a developed point such as the removed material becomes waste swarf that is not part of the finished component, or that the starting block must be larger than the finished part. [3 marks]
note: F2: The answer key must not state that swarf cannot be recovered.

expect: The main disadvantage is material waste — the swarf and offcuts removed cannot be recovered, increasing material cost.
value: The main disadvantage is material waste — the swarf and offcuts removed do not form part of the component, increasing material cost.
note: F2: Removes the false claim that all removed material is unrecoverable.

find: A one-word process type without explanation scores only 1 mark; a type plus a clear mechanism scores full marks.
replace: For an ‘explain’ question, name the process type and say how it changes the material.
note: F3: R014 gives no universal mark allocation for an explain response.

expect: What are the six types of manufacturing process named in the OCR R041 specification?
value: What are the six types of manufacturing process named in the OCR R014 specification?
note: F4: Correct unit code.

expect: Name the two finishing processes listed in the OCR R041 specification.
value: Name the two finishing processes listed in the OCR R014 specification.
note: F4: Correct unit code.

find: Powder metallurgy compacts ceramic or metal powder at very high pressure then sinters (heats without fully melting) to bond particles — used for ceramic products and porous components such as self-lubricating bearings.
replace: Powder metallurgy for ceramic products compacts ceramic powder at very high pressure, then sinters it without fully melting to bond the particles.
note: F5: Aligns powder metallurgy with the specified ceramic-product scope.

find: Shaping processes (sand casting, die casting, injection moulding, powder metallurgy) pour or inject material into a mould — sand casting uses an expendable mould while die casting uses a permanent reusable steel die.
replace: Shaping processes include sand casting, die casting, injection moulding and powder metallurgy. Sand casting uses an expendable mould while die casting uses a permanent reusable steel die.
note: F5: Powder metallurgy does not pour or inject material into a mould.

expect: Which two shearing tools are permitted in the OCR R041 specification?
value: Which two shearing tools are permitted in the OCR R014 specification?
note: F6: Correct unit code.

expect: Name the four shaping processes listed in the OCR R041 specification.
value: Name the four shaping processes listed in the OCR R014 specification.
note: F6: Correct unit code.

find: Ferrous metals contain iron and are magnetic and prone to corrosion unless protected.
replace: Ferrous metals contain iron and are often magnetic, but magnetism and corrosion resistance depend on the alloy.
note: F7: Stainless-steel magnetism varies by grade.

find: All contain iron, are magnetic, and corrode unless protected — except stainless steel, whose chromium content forms a self-healing protective oxide layer.
replace: All contain iron. Their magnetism and corrosion resistance depend on the alloy; stainless steel's chromium content forms a self-healing protective oxide layer.
note: F7: Removes the false universal magnetic and corrosion claim.

expect: Ferrous metals contain iron as the primary element, making them magnetic and prone to corrosion without protection.
value: Ferrous metals contain iron. Their magnetism and corrosion resistance depend on the alloy.
note: F7: Magnetism and corrosion resistance are grade-dependent.

expect: A metal that contains iron as its primary constituent, making it susceptible to rusting unless protected by alloying or coating.
value: A metal or alloy that contains iron. Its magnetism and corrosion resistance depend on the alloy.
note: F7: Avoids treating all ferrous materials as magnetic and rust-prone.

find: Alloys are single-phase metallic mixtures; composites retain physically distinct constituent materials — do not confuse them in exam answers.
replace: Alloys are metallic mixtures; composites retain physically distinct constituent materials — do not confuse them in exam answers.
note: F8: An alloy can contain more than one phase.

expect: Name the four thermosetting polymers listed in the OCR R041 specification.
value: Name the four thermosetting polymers listed in the OCR R014 specification.
note: F9: Correct unit code.

expect: What are the two cost components specified in OCR R041 for material selection?
value: What are the two cost components specified in OCR R014 for material selection?
note: F10: Correct unit code.

expect: List the five material selection criteria covered in OCR R041 Topic Area 2.3.
value: List the five material selection criteria covered in OCR R014 Topic Area 2.3.
note: F10: Correct unit code.
F11: R014 names mass manufacture, not continuous production.
F11: R014 names mass manufacture, not continuous production.

expect: The three scales are one-off production, batch production, and mass (continuous) production, each suited to different volumes.
value: The three scales are one-off production, batch production, and mass production, each suited to different volumes.
note: F11: Uses the listed R014 scale term.

find: reduction in defects (no human error during cutting)
replace: reduction in defects through consistent machine control
note: F12: CAM can reduce defects but does not eliminate human error.

find: The tolerance is calculated from an orthographic engineering drawing: maximum acceptable dimension = nominal + upper deviation; minimum acceptable dimension = nominal − lower deviation.
replace: From an engineering drawing, the maximum acceptable dimension is the nominal size plus the upper deviation. The minimum acceptable dimension is the nominal size plus the stated lower deviation; when it is negative, this means subtraction.
note: F13: Corrects the signed lower-deviation calculation.

find: Go/no-go gauges are purpose-made limit gauges: the 'go' end must pass through the feature (confirming it is not undersized) while the 'no-go' end must not pass (confirming it is not oversized).
replace: Go/no-go gauges are purpose-made limit gauges. For a hole, the ‘go’ plug must enter (confirming the hole is not undersized) and the ‘no-go’ plug must not enter (confirming it is not oversized).
note: F14: The stated rule is for a hole and plug gauge.

expect: A go/no-go gauge is a limit gauge that gives an instant pass/fail check; the go end must pass and the no-go end must not, confirming the part is within tolerance.
value: A go/no-go gauge gives a pass/fail check. For a hole, the go plug enters and the no-go plug does not; it is fast for production.
note: F14: Specifies the correct plug-gauge use case.

find: Respiratory protection (dust mask or respirator) is needed when sanding, grinding composite materials (which produce carcinogenic fibres), spray painting or powder coating.
replace: Respiratory protection is needed when sanding, grinding composite materials that can release hazardous dust, spray painting or powder coating.
note: F15: Carbon-fibre handling hazards are not established as carcinogenic fibres.

expect:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies the specific hazards (fine CRP dust — carcinogenic; noise above 85 dB(A); eye hazard from particles), assesses what PPE can offer (FFP3 respirator to filter fine particles; ear defenders; safety spectacles — these address the immediate personal exposure), then critically evaluates the limitations (PPE relies on consistent correct wearing and fit; it does not remove the dust from the environment so other workers nearby are also at risk; hearing protection only works if worn at all times in the noise zone; grinding CRP is a cumulative long-term health risk where any lapse in PPE has lasting consequences). Argues that engineering controls should be primary: local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at the grinding point removes particles before they become airborne; acoustic enclosures reduce noise at source; these protect all workers regardless of individual PPE compliance. Reaches a clear substantiated judgement — PPE is necessary but insufficient alone; LEV and enclosure are essential primary controls.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to CRP grinding context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about PPE or hazards with little development. [8 marks]
value:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies the specific hazards (fine CRP dust; noise above 85 dB(A); eye hazard from particles), assesses what PPE can offer (FFP3 respirator to filter fine particles; ear defenders; safety spectacles — these address the immediate personal exposure), then critically evaluates the limitations (PPE relies on consistent correct wearing and fit; it does not remove the dust from the environment so other workers nearby are also at risk; hearing protection only works if worn at all times in the noise zone; grinding CRP is a cumulative long-term health risk where any lapse in PPE has lasting consequences). Argues that engineering controls should be primary: local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at the grinding point removes particles before they become airborne; acoustic enclosures reduce noise at source; these protect all workers regardless of individual PPE compliance. Reaches a clear substantiated judgement — PPE is necessary but insufficient alone; LEV and enclosure are essential primary controls.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to CRP grinding context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about PPE or hazards with little development. [8 marks]
note: F15: Removes the unsupported carcinogenic claim from the answer key.

expect: FFP3 respirator to filter carcinogenic fine particles
value: FFP3 respirator to filter fine airborne particles
note: F15: Removes the unsupported carcinogenic claim.

expect: An FFP3 respirator is needed to filter the fine carcinogenic particles generated when grinding carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CRP) components.
value: An FFP3 respirator can filter fine airborne particles generated when grinding carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CRP) components.
note: F15: Removes the unsupported carcinogenic claim.

expect:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that constructs the argument for responsibility (consumers buy the final product believing the company endorses all aspects of its production; the company profits from lower costs partly achieved through poor conditions; reputational and legal risks — supply chain transparency legislation (e.g. UK Modern Slavery Act) means companies can be held accountable; the company has leverage to demand standards as a major customer). Then challenges this: the company cannot directly control independent suppliers in other countries; different legal frameworks mean what is legal abroad may be unacceptable at home; the cost of supply chain auditing is significant; forcing higher wages may make the supply uneconomic and shift production to less-auditable suppliers. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. the company has both a moral and legal responsibility, but must act through specific enforceable supplier codes of conduct, regular auditing and willingness to exit relationships with non-compliant suppliers, rather than assuming responsibility can be delegated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to the scenario and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development or evaluation. [8 marks]
value:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that constructs the argument for responsibility (consumers buy the final product believing the company endorses all aspects of its production; the company profits from lower costs partly achieved through poor conditions; reputational risks and, for some UK companies, legal reporting duties under supply chain transparency legislation (e.g. UK Modern Slavery Act); the company has leverage to demand standards as a major customer). Then challenges this: the company cannot directly control independent suppliers in other countries; different legal frameworks mean what is legal abroad may be unacceptable at home; the cost of supply chain auditing is significant; forcing higher wages may make the supply uneconomic and shift production to less-auditable suppliers. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. the company has a moral responsibility and may have legal reporting duties, but must act through specific enforceable supplier codes of conduct, regular auditing and willingness to exit relationships with non-compliant suppliers, rather than assuming responsibility can be delegated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to the scenario and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development or evaluation. [8 marks]
note: F16: Corrects the limited reporting duty under the Modern Slavery Act.
